Put a field of cultivated wheat beside a stand of wild grass and the difference is plain: the crop plants vary more among themselves than the wild ones do. Livestock show the same thing. Two dairy cows from one herd can differ in size, color, temperament, and yield far more than two deer from one forest.

That is no coincidence, and breeders picking out odd individuals cannot account for all of it. It seems to come from the conditions domesticated species live under. A wild population meets a fairly stable set of pressures over long stretches of time. A cultivated one is carried between climates, fed on new diets, sheltered from predators, and bred in ways it would never manage on its own. Those changes in circumstance appear to loosen whatever holds a species to its typical form. Some researchers have suggested that a rich food supply plays a particular part, and that seems plausible, though it is hard to separate from everything else that changes when an animal is brought under human care.

Two things about the effect are clearer. It is slow to appear, and it does not readily switch off. A species may need several generations under new conditions before it starts producing noticeable variants. Once it starts, it tends to keep going. Our oldest crops still throw off new strains, and breeders are still reshaping our oldest domestic animals today.

I was born on a small farm outside a market town in eastern Maryland. When, I cannot say. No one wrote it down, or if someone did, I never saw the record.

That was the ordinary case for enslaved people in that part of the country. Most could not have told you the year of their birth, let alone the day, and the men who owned them preferred it so. Dates were kept for livestock and for account books, not for people who were themselves entries in the account book. When anyone did try to place a birth, they reckoned by the seasons: around planting, around harvest, the year the cherries came in early.

As a child this bothered me more than I could explain. The white children knew how old they were and said so freely. I did not understand what made my case different, and I was not permitted to ask. My owner took any question of that kind for insolence, the first symptom of a slave who was thinking too much.

My best guess now is that I am in my late twenties. I have that figure only because I once overheard him mention my age in passing, and I have been counting forward from it ever since.

Since I have brought up my father, a few words about him. He was a sound man physically, of average height but solidly built, and stronger than most. He had a number of small talents he never made much of. He could sketch well. He knew enough music to play a few hymns on the fiddle, and he had a good singing voice, so on evenings when the shop was closed he would sometimes play and sing for the family, which we all enjoyed. He was handy in a general way too, and could pick up almost any tradesman's tools and use them competently.

But what people valued most in him was his judgment. He had a practical, level-headed way of thinking through a problem, domestic or public, and the neighbors came to rely on it. He never held office. With a large family to support and not much money, he could not afford time away from his trade. Even so, I remember prominent men from the town and from his congregation calling at the house to ask his view on some matter then under discussion, and listening to his answer with real attention. Private people brought him their disputes as well, and he was often asked to arbitrate between parties who could not settle a quarrel on their own.

output_text:
The simplest way to see what government is for is to imagine doing without one. Picture a handful of people landed in some remote place, cut off from every other society. They stand in for the first inhabitants of any country. The first thing they will do, before anyone thinks about rules or leaders, is form a community, because none of them can manage alone. One person's needs run far ahead of one person's strength, and few people can stand long isolation. So each of them will look to the others for help, and each will be asked for help in return.

Take shelter. Four or five people working together can put up a decent cabin in a clearing within a season. One person could spend a whole lifetime on it and never finish. He might fell the trees, but he could not haul the logs, and if he somehow hauled them, he could not raise them into walls by himself. All the while he has to eat, so every day the work stops for hunting or gathering, and every new need drags him off in another direction. If he falls ill or breaks a leg, he is finished. The injury itself would not kill him. It would stop him doing the work that keeps him alive.

output_text:
Most of us worry far more than our circumstances call for. We could hand off a good share of the care we spend on ourselves and lose nothing by it, because the world is built to accommodate our weak points as well as our strong ones. For some people, constant anxiety has become a chronic condition that no reassurance cures.

Part of the trouble is that we overrate our own work. Look at how much gets done without us. If we were laid up for a month, things would mostly carry on. Yet we stand guard all day, trusting nothing we cannot control, and only at night, worn out, do we reluctantly let go and admit that tomorrow is uncertain. We are so committed to living as we live that our habits become sacred to us, and we cannot picture doing otherwise. This is the only way, we tell ourselves. But there are as many ways to live as there are directions to walk from a single point. Change looks like a miracle from the outside, and yet it is going on all the time, in small steps, in everyone. Real knowledge, as an old proverb has it, is knowing what you know and knowing what you do not. And once one person has turned a hope into a fact, sooner or later everyone builds on it.

By the time I could read the river the way I could read a page, and knew every bend and snag and sandbar on it by heart, I had a skill that would earn me a living. The skill cost me something, and the cost was permanent. The river stopped being beautiful to me.

I can still remember one sunset from my first weeks on the water, before any of that had happened. The whole surface had gone red, fading to gold in the middle distance, and a single dark log drifted through the gold like a stroke of ink. Off to one side a long slanting streak caught the light and sparkled. Somewhere else the water churned in slow rings that ran through every color you could name. Where the red was palest there was a patch of glassy water marked with faint circles and radiating lines, as if someone had drawn them with a fine pen. The left bank was heavy forest, and the shadow it threw across the water was cut in one place by a bright ruffled path that looked like beaten silver. Above the treeline a dead tree with one living branch stood against the sky, and that branch caught the last full light of the sun and seemed to burn. There were curves and reflections, wooded bluffs, softened distances, and over all of it the light kept shifting as the sun went down, so that every minute the scene rearranged itself into something new. I had never seen anything like it. And I did not know, then, that I was seeing it for the last time in that way.
